title: A 1571 Letter Undercuts the Hoax Theory Around the "Other Voynich Manuscript" and Reveals a Terrified Scribe

content:
Two sheets covered in the unreadable script of the Rohonc Codex have turned up inside a letter dated 1571 in a Hungarian noble family’s archive. The find pushes back the date of the manuscript and sketches its author: an educated scribe, shy and afraid of being laughed at.

Some medieval books can’t be read by anyone, and one of them has become almost a trademark of the genre: the Voynich manuscript, kept at Yale University and dated to the 15th century. It has inspired novels and theories of every kind. Specialists often place another volume right behind it on the list of enigmas, the Rohonc Codex. Far fewer people have heard of it. A Hungarian team has now found a document that forces a rewrite of much of its history.

The codex is kept at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in Budapest. It is a small paper book of 448 pages, each one smaller than a postcard (roughly 4 by 5 inches, or 10 by 12 centimetres). The pages are filled with unknown symbols and illustrated with more than eighty drawings. The first and last pages are missing, so even the original order is uncertain. The leather binding dates from the 19th century and says nothing about the book’s past.

Its name comes from Rohonc, today Rechnitz in Austria, where the noble Batthyány family had its residence. The book surfaced in 1838, when Count Gusztáv Batthyány donated his library to the Academy. At first it caused great excitement, because some saw in its signs proof of a very ancient Hungarian script. By the end of the 19th century the enthusiasm had turned into suspicion, and the codex was branded a forgery. According to the authors of the new study, that verdict left the manuscript largely ignored by scholars for about a century, with a few exceptions.

Things began to change in the early 2010s. Two Hungarian researchers, Gábor Tokai and Levente Zoltán Király, proposed a reading of the text. They used long repeated passages to put the pages back in order, then compared passages with well-known Bible stories until they had built a dictionary. The authors of the new paper say about 98% of the content can now be identified. They add that part of it rests on educated reconstruction and that the grammar is only partly understood.

Whole sentences appear in the text, among them the Lord’s Prayer, the Hail Mary and the institution of the Eucharist (the moment at the Last Supper when Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples). The researchers stress that these matches were not guessed from the drawings. They emerged from the internal logic of the system. Gaps and inconsistencies in vocabulary and grammar still feed the scepticism of some colleagues.

Even with the content largely clarified, basic questions remained. When was the codex written? When did it reach the Batthyány library, and who owned it? What language did its author think in? Was it the work of one person?

The letter that sat in an archive

The answer came from an unglamorous direction. The Hungarian National Archives are digitising 16th-century correspondence, and the historian Béla Hanák, who was researching something else, noticed a letter with an enclosure. He alerted the codex specialists. The discovery is reported in a 2026 paper in the journal Cryptologia, signed by Benedek Láng of Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Dóra Bobory, Levente Zoltán Király and Gábor Tokai.

The letter sits in the Batthyány family collection. It was written by Farkas Porhócs, administrator of the Torony estate, to his lord, Boldizsár Batthyány. Two sheets came with it, four pages in all, written in the same symbols as the Rohonc Codex.

So how did it go unnoticed? According to the authors, the blame seems to fall on Béla Iványi, the archivist who organised the family papers before the Second World War. He underlined in pencil a mention of some books and summed up the enclosure as two papers in Glagolitic script, the oldest known Slavic alphabet, probably created in the 9th century. He also described “primitive drawings” of church towers in an Eastern Slavic style. The authors call this a striking mistake even for an inexperienced researcher, and they can’t explain it.

Let’s look at what the letter says. It is written in 16th-century Hungarian. Porhócs reports that the deák (a scribe, often a noble’s personal secretary) does not want to travel up to the lord’s main residences. The man says Batthyány would make him write a letter there that, in his own words, he would not know how to write. He fears the other secretaries would laugh at him and never leave him in peace. He also claims to be very ill, with one side of his body burning and the other freezing.

Even so, the scribe would be willing to appear before his lord, and to bring “the books”, if Batthyány came down to Torony and the preacher guaranteed that nobody would harm him. Porhócs sends a sample of the man’s writing, which he had composed at Torony. He explains that he can’t send the scribe himself, because the man is on the lands of a nobleman named Zrínyi.

Same hand, different sheets

The authors first had to check that the letter and the sheets really belonged together. They appear to. The letter was folded like an envelope, and one of the sheets fits inside it exactly. The other, slightly larger, still carries the crease from being folded to fit. The damage on both sheets also predates their insertion in the letter, so they had been used before.

Could they be loose pages from the codex itself? The authors say no. The new sheets are squarer and a little smaller than the codex pages. The handwriting has a different scale, with lines spaced further apart and a wider, lower writing area. No watermark is visible to compare with the codex’s paper, which comes from northern Italy, but paper and ink look very similar.

From this the authors draw an important conclusion: whoever invented this script used it in more than one manuscript. One of the samples carries a 16th-century date, so the script survived in at least two independent contexts. In their view, that definitively rules out the idea that the codex is a 19th-century fraud. Other scholars may weigh that wording differently.

A frightened scribe

The recipient was no minor figure. Boldizsár Batthyány (1542–1590) was a major landowner in western Hungary with a taste for botany, medicine and alchemy. He was an early reader of Paracelsus (the Swiss physician and alchemist), a friend of the Flemish botanist Carolus Clusius, whom he helped to study the local flora, and he corresponded with scholars across Europe. He also built up a notable library.

His life played out on a turbulent frontier, with wars against the Ottomans, religious persecution and epidemics. The letter was written a little over three months before the Battle of Lepanto, the great naval clash between the Ottoman fleet and a Christian alliance. One of the study’s co-authors, the historian Dóra Bobory, wrote a biography of the count published in 2009.

Torony belonged to the Batthyány family at the time. In the early 17th century it passed to the Zrínyi family, relatives and neighbours with similar religious views. From that world comes the scribe, whom the study describes as an educated person, neither an untrained genius nor a member of a sect, as has sometimes been suggested. The authors think he came from central Europe, perhaps Hungary, Germany or Croatia, but they warn that there is no way to be sure.

Travelling students, known as peregrini, often turned up at the courts of the Hungarian nobility. A search of databases of such travellers found no matching name. No other letters from Porhócs or the Zrínyi family mention the scribe, and much of the Batthyány archive was destroyed in 1944–45 and again in 1956.

One detail strikes the authors as odd. The text of the codex is consistent with Catholic doctrine, while Batthyány’s court was probably Lutheran, with some Calvinist leanings. His fear of mockery may have had something to do with that, although they insist it is only a hypothesis and the letter says nothing about the man’s religion. It is also curious that a Catholic would ask for the protection of a Protestant preacher. Later letters from Porhócs, dated 1572, describe that preacher leaving Torony and local peasants looking for a Catholic priest. The authors admit these references are vague.

A date that no longer fits

Before the discovery, the codex was placed in the 1590s. In a note near the end of the book, the researchers read “1,560 years since the Ascension of Christ”, which would correspond to 1593. Other clues seemed to agree. The text mentions earthquakes that recall those of 1590 near Vienna, and one passage appears to depend on the Károli Bible, the first complete Hungarian translation, also published in 1590.

The 1571 letter forces a rethink. The authors suggest the book may have been written slowly over several years, or received additions at the end. They also find internal signs that much of the text already existed in 1571. The formula that opens the chapters appears already developed on the new sheets, and its evolution can be followed through the codex up to page 65. A symbol on the new sheets for “bed” looks like a shortened version of a longer symbol, “stretcher”, which appears around page 161. From this they deduce that the codex was already written at least as far as those pages in 1571. This is the authors’ own reasoning, not an independent dating.

The date matters for a specific reason. It had been suggested that the inventor of the script drew on Western descriptions of Chinese writing, such as the treatise by the Dominican friar Gaspar da Cruz, published in 1569, or its Spanish summary printed in Rome in 1585. If the script predates 1571, its author would have had to know that treatise almost as soon as it came off the press, or use another source that has yet to be identified. The alternative is that he devised, on his own, a writing system that could be read in several languages. For comparison, Esperanto would not appear until 1887, and the authors argue that the Rohonc script predates most known attempts at an artificial language or script by decades.

The new sheets can be read with the same decipherment method as the codex, which the authors take as reinforcing that reading. All four pages come from the Gospel of Luke, something the authors prefer not to interpret. Some symbols don’t appear in the codex at all, such as a variant of “lamb” or a genitive sign (a mark showing possession, like the ’s in “the lord’s”) placed after the word.

What remains open

The study, which closes with more questions than answers, is signed by Láng, Bobory, Király and Tokai. It is not known why the scribe approached Batthyány in particular, or what the two men’s relationship was. It is not known what the script was created for: a cipher to shelter from religious persecution, a commercial invention, or simple intellectual curiosity.

The authors also wonder whether the scribe could have come from an isolated monastic community in southern Europe, which would explain his conservative tone and his reputation as an eccentric. They ask whether the model for the script was a natural language he knew, or some idea of artificial languages circulating in central Europe that has not yet been identified.

And it is still unclear whether the system is a language with sounds of its own or only an artificial script. On that last point, the authors offer no answer.

A version of this article is also available in Spanish: Léelo en español

SOURCES

Láng, B., Bobory, D., Király, L. Z., & Tokai, G. (2026). New evidence on the Rohonc Codex: authorship, provenance, and script continuity. Cryptologia, 1–24. doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2026.2711207
